A.title: Join FP10 in full only with a tougher refund rule and a hard cap
A.answer: Make the refund rule the price of joining. The UK is refunded when its grants underperform by 16%; Switzerland's trigger is 8% (s1). UK negotiators should win a stricter rule before signing, and the Treasury should cap the contribution at the £2.2 billion a year already budgeted (s1). Science Works puts the likeliest gap at £1.2 billion in 2029-30 (s1), so the deal should say who pays any overrun, with a review point as the 2025 spending review already allows (s2). No gap is met from NHS, school or lab budgets. It worked if the signed text sets the trigger, yearly bills stay within budget, and UK success in European Research Council and Marie Curie grants holds (s2).

B.title: Give an independent science board the FP10 budget and the deal
B.answer: Parliament should hand the FP10 decision to a ring-fenced research board, instead of leaving it to year-by-year Treasury haggling. The government would set the board a fixed envelope, starting from the £2.2 billion a year already budgeted (s1). The board would negotiate the entry terms, including a higher refund trigger than today's 16% (s1), and choose between full membership and Excellent Science only, which the thinktank says costs £2.4 billion a year less (s1). It would publish costs yearly and could not draw on NHS or school budgets, a limit 51 simulated citizens backed. You'd know it worked if the real gap stays inside the envelope, against a projected £1.2 billion in 2029-30 (s1).
